To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the tooth microenvironment is capable of supporting osteoclast formation in the absence of osteoblasts or osteoclast precursers, and that this process is regulated by stellate reticular cells, which secrete PTHrP, which then stimulates osteoclast differentiation via osteoblasts in the dental follicle.
PTHrP induces osteoclast formation in dental crypt cells in a manner that is analogous to osteoblast-mediated osteoclastogenesis in the peripheral skeleton.
PTHrP induces spontaneous osteoclastic bone formation via a parathyroid hormone-like paracrine cascade.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular mechanisms of PTHrPs role in regulating osteoclasts.
understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms by which PTHrP regulates tooth eruption and the development of dental tissues.
the mechanisms of osteoclast regulation and tooth eruption.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PTHrP is a potent inducer of osteoclast differentiation and function in the dental microenvironment.
PTHrP is a critical regulator of osteoclast differentiation and function in the dental microenvironment.
PTHrP induces osteoclast differentiation in the tooth via a paracrinemediated cascade involving the expression of osteoclastogenic factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PTHrP is the primary regulator of osteoclast differentiation and function in the microenvironment surrounding the teeth.
tooth eruption is dependent on a parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP)-induced osteoclastic bone-resorption cascade that is mediated through the dental follicle cells.
tooth eruption requires PTHrP action in the dental follicle to stimulate osteoclast formation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PTHrP is an important factor in regulating osteoclastogenesis in the microenvironment around the tooth.
PTHrP is an important regulator of osteoclast differentiation and function in vivo, and that PTHrPs may be important for tooth eruption.
